511.quote_or_event: “The swans peck at the diamonds and pearls, while the crane chases after frogs.”
511.explanation: Guru Arjan contrasts the swan, which by its nature picks out what is precious, with the crane, which by its nature goes after what is base.
511.tie_back: The Kural says to employ the one who, after weighing good and harm, is by nature drawn to the good; Guru Arjan's swan is exactly such a nature, choosing pearls over frogs.
511.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 960, Raag Raamkalee, Raamkalee Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
511._accuracy_note: Good on a settled disposition toward the good; Guru Arjan contrasts the devout and the worldly rather than describing how to choose an agent.

512.quote_or_event: Guru Amar Das organised the Sikh congregations into twenty-two districts (manjis) whose leaders passed on the disciples' offerings. When Guru Ram Das began the costly work of digging the sacred pool at Amritsar and building the Harimandar, Sikhs were asked to set aside a tenth of their income (dasvandh), and masands were appointed to collect it and bring it to the Guru.
512.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism describes how the early Gurus built up regular channels of income for the community and turned them into lasting institutions such as the shrine and the langar.
512.tie_back: The Kural wants an administrator who widens the sources of revenue and turns them into growing prosperity; the early Sikh system of districts, tithes and collectors did just that for the community.
512.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Dasvandh' (paraphrase)
512._accuracy_note: A reasonable parallel on building revenue channels, but dasvandh is religious giving for community welfare, not state revenue, and the Kural's third duty of removing obstacles is not covered.

513.quote_or_event: As a young man Guru Nanak moved to Sultanpur and worked as a clerk in the Lodi administration. The janamsakhis, the traditional accounts of his life, remember him in these years for his honesty and devotion to truth.
513.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project notes Guru Nanak's government post at Sultanpur and the janamsakhi tradition of his honesty in it.
513.tie_back: The Kural trusts the one who combines loyalty, knowledge, clear judgement and freedom from greed; the janamsakhis present the young Nanak as just such an honest official.
513.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'Guru Nanak' (paraphrase; janamsakhi tradition)
513._accuracy_note: Next-best: the employment is historical, but the emphasis on his honesty comes from hagiographic janamsakhi tradition, and the source does not detail the Kural's four qualities.

514.quote_or_event: The masands, appointed by Guru Arjan to preach and to collect the community's offerings, were at first chosen for their piety and devotion. As time passed many grew neglectful of their office and took to enriching themselves, until Guru Gobind Singh charged them with corruption and oppression, punished the guilty and abolished the institution.
514.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism traces how agents who had been carefully selected were changed by the power and wealth their office brought.
514.tie_back: The Kural warns that even people tested in every way often turn out differently once they are doing the work; the masands, chosen for piety, were corrupted by their office.
514.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Masands' (paraphrase)
514._accuracy_note: A close historical illustration of well-chosen officials changing in office; the decline happened over generations rather than in the individuals first appointed.

515.quote_or_event: Guru Nanak had two sons, yet before he died he appointed one of his faithful followers as his successor in leading the community, naming him Guru Angad, the 'limb' of Guru Nanak.
515.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project records that leadership passed to a proven disciple rather than to the Guru's own sons.
515.tie_back: The Kural says a task should go to one who knows how to do it and can see it through, never to someone because he is dear; Guru Nanak passed over his own sons for a faithful disciple.
515.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'Guru Nanak' (paraphrase)
515._accuracy_note: A strong fit on competence and devotion over closeness; the succession was spiritual leadership, not a worldly task, and the source does not describe how Angad was tested.

516.quote_or_event: “One who reflects upon his allotted span of life, becomes the slave of God.”
516.explanation: Guru Nanak praises the person who thinks about the time he has been given and uses it for its true purpose.
516.tie_back: The Kural asks that the doer and the deed be weighed and then matched to the right time; Guru Nanak likewise asks that one's time be considered before it is spent.
516.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 84, Siree Raag, Siree Raag Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
516._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared element is attention to time, while the Kural's method of matching agent, task and moment has no direct Gurbani counterpart that I could find.

517.quote_or_event: When Guru Arjan compiled the first definitive collection of Sikh scripture, he entrusted the writing of the text to Bhai Gurdas, a senior member of his congregation, who served as scribe of the Adi Granth. The work was finished in 1604 and installed in the Darbar Sahib at Amritsar.
517.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project records that the Guru chose a learned and trusted disciple for the most important writing task of the early community.
517.tie_back: The Kural says that once one has decided that this person will do this task by these means, the task should be handed over to him; Guru Arjan handed the writing of the scripture to Bhai Gurdas.
517.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'The Sikh Scripture' (paraphrase)
517._accuracy_note: A clear historical case of entrusting a task to a fitting person; the source does not describe Guru Arjan's reasoning or how fully the work was left to Bhai Gurdas.

518.quote_or_event: In 1708 at Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh initiated Banda Singh into the Khalsa and, before sending him north to the Punjab, gave him a drum, a banner and five arrows as emblems of authority, with five Sikhs to accompany him.
518.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism records that the Guru gave Banda Singh both a mission and visible signs of the authority needed to carry it out.
518.tie_back: The Kural says that once a person's fitness for a task is known, he should be made fully responsible for it with the authority that goes with it; Guru Gobind Singh gave Banda Singh both.
518.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Banda Singh Bahadur', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
518._accuracy_note: A strong parallel for delegating authority with the commission; the source says little about how the Guru judged Banda Singh fit, and the appointment came soon after their meeting.

519.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, all happiness vanishes. … Slandering the Saints, all one's influence vanishes.”
519.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan lists the losses that come to one who speaks ill of the devoted: peace, standing and influence all depart.
519.tie_back: The Kural says fortune leaves the ruler who grows suspicious of a servant devoted to his work; Guru Arjan says influence and happiness leave the one who turns against the devoted.
519.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 13), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
519._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both tie the loss of fortune to wronging the devoted, but Guru Arjan speaks of slandering saints, not of a ruler misreading a loyal servant's closeness.

520.quote_or_event: “The kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs; they go out and awaken the sleeping people to harass them.”
520.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a realm where rulers prey on the people and their officials, left unchecked, go out to harass ordinary folk.
520.tie_back: The Kural says a king must watch his officials every day, because the world goes crooked when they do; Guru Nanak shows the world that results when officials are not held straight.
520.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Malaar Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
520._accuracy_note: A strong fit on corrupt officials corrupting society; Guru Nanak denounces the condition rather than prescribing the daily supervision the Kural recommends.
